questions.prompt: What is the difference between a source-code dependency and a runtime dependency?

options.text: A source-code dependency is what your code imports/mentions at compile time; a runtime dependency is which code calls which at run time
A source-code dependency only exists in compiled languages
A runtime dependency is always the reverse of coupling

questions.explanation: Source-code dependencies (imports) are fixed at compile time; runtime dependencies are actual calls. They often point the same way — but architecture's key trick is making them oppose.

questions.prompt: A module has many INCOMING dependencies (many things depend on it). This makes it:

options.text: Stable — costly to change because much relies on it

questions.explanation: Many incoming (afferent) dependencies make a module stable: changing it disrupts everything that depends on it, so you avoid changing it often.

questions.prompt: You want low coupling and ______ cohesion.
questions.explanation: Good design aims for loose coupling (modules don't rely on each other's internals) and high cohesion (a module's parts belong together).

questions.prompt: Which are signs of LOOSE coupling? Select all that apply.

options.text: A class depends on a small interface rather than a concrete implementation
You can swap a collaborator (e.g., for a test fake) without editing the class
A class constructs its collaborators with `new` and calls their private helpers
A change to a collaborator's internals doesn't break the class

questions.explanation: Loose coupling means depending on small stable contracts and being able to swap implementations. Constructing concretes and using their internals is tight coupling.

questions.prompt: Order these from MOST volatile to MOST stable in a healthy dependency chain (dependencies should point from volatile toward stable).
questions.explanation: Volatile details (frameworks) should depend toward stable policy (entities). Stability increases as you move inward, which is why dependencies point that way.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

pairs.right: How much one module relies on another's details
How well the parts inside a module belong together
Incoming dependencies — things that depend on you
Outgoing dependencies — things you depend on

questions.explanation: Coupling is between modules; cohesion is within one. Afferent = incoming, efferent = outgoing.
